name: The Capitol Park Moon Tree

location.address: North side of the California State Capitol, beside the northeast security pavilion, 10th and L Streets, Sacramento

verified_sources: https://capitolmuseum.ca.gov/images/pdf/CapitolParkTreeBooklet.pdf (via web.archive.org, State Capitol Museum Capitol Park Tree Guide, updated 2016-09-01, p.8)
access: Free. Capitol Park is open to the public daily; the tree stands on the lawn at the northeast corner of the Capitol building, by the security pavilion. Capitol Annex construction is under way nearby, so some paths may be fenced.
how_to_recognise: A tall, narrow coast redwood on the lawn at the north-east corner of the Capitol, beside the security pavilion and behind the Sisters of Mercy sculpture; the only redwood there that is much taller than the rest.
verify_notes: Coast redwood grown from a seed carried around the moon on Apollo 14 (1971, command module pilot Stuart Roosa, seeds from the US Forest Service). NASA NSSDCA: seeds collected near Soquel CA in 1966; seedling shipped 1976-04-02 from the Institute of Forest Genetics, Placerville; planted April 1976 (page gives April 20 with a question mark), about 2 ft tall then. NASA (page updated 2024-05-20): about 120 ft tall, canopy about 40 ft; says the Annex pavilion plans were designed to ensure the tree's safety. Waymarking (visitor, last visit 2021-09-26): 120 ft, canopy 40 ft, GPS 38.57698, -121.49297; NASA 38 34.616 N 121 29.581 W = 38.57693, -121.49302, within about 10 m of each other: published GPS positions, pin recorded as confirmed. State Capitol Museum tree guide (2016) p.8 lists the Moon Tree, a Coast Redwood, in Section 2 North (East). Life check: CBS Sacramento (2023, via search summary, article not fetched) reports Moon Tree and Civil War grove protected in place during the Capitol Annex project; NASA 2024 update describes it standing. No dated photo of the trunk itself seen (lifecheck.py: nothing within range; iNaturalist none). Flag: confirm the tree still stands after annex works. Sacramento's only Moon Tree, one of seven in California. height_m 37 from NASA's 120 ft. The Capitol Annex project threatened dozens of other Capitol Park trees (DGS estimate 20 to 30 affected, advocates up to 100).

name: The Deodar Cedars of the Capitol's west front

location.address: West side of the California State Capitol, 10th Street between L and N, Sacramento

verified_sources: https://capitolmuseum.ca.gov/images/pdf/CapitolParkTreeBooklet.pdf (via web.archive.org, State Capitol Museum Capitol Park Tree Guide, updated 2016-09-01, pp.3, 6, 7)
https://annex.assembly.ca.gov/sites/annex.assembly.ca.gov/files/Capitol%20Tree%20Map.pdf (adapted from California State Parks Capitol Park Tree Listing, 2016-01-14)

official_register.name: California State Capitol Museum, Capitol Park Tree Guide

access: Free. Capitol Park is open to the public; the cedars line the lawn at the west entrance of the Capitol.
how_to_recognise: A row of ten tall, drooping-branched cedars on the lawn in front of the Capitol's west entrance; the largest of the ten is the state's largest deodar.
verify_notes: State Capitol Museum tree guide (2016): ten Deodar Cedars line the west side of the Capitol; several are part of the Capitol's original twelve planted in 1872; one of the ten is the largest deodar in California (state champion; the guide takes champion data from the Cal Poly California Big Trees Registry). Which of the ten is the champion is not stated, so the pin is approximate and sits at the register champion coordinate (finding aid only, not cited), inside a 50 m radius of the west lawn. No girth or height recorded: the Cal Poly lead row's units are ambiguous (published in inches and feet, lead stores 625 and 31) and a Cal State Stanislaus figure (228 in circumference, 98 ft, seen only in a search summary) was not fetched. One official source (owner of the ground), flagged 'one source'. Life: iNaturalist observation 2026-10-15 near the register coordinate (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/408579777), not proof it is the champion itself. Annex construction put dozens of Capitol Park trees at risk (DGS estimate 20 to 30 affected); no report of cedar removal found.
